title: Directed Euler Paths: In-Degree/Out-Degree Characterization
description: Proves the directed analogue of Euler's theorem: a digraph has an Eulerian circuit iff every vertex has indegree = outdegree, and an Eulerian path iff exactly one vertex has outdegree-indegree=1 (start) and exactly one has indegree-outdegree=1 (end). Defines directed graphs from scratch with degree properties and verified examples. 2 axioms for the sufficiency directions.

meta.author: Lean Genius
meta.assumptions: 2 axioms: directed_euler_circuit_sufficient (balanced digraph → Eulerian circuit exists) and directed_euler_path_sufficient (exactly one source + one sink → Eulerian path exists). The necessary conditions are fully proved; the sufficiency requires an Eulerian circuit construction algorithm (e.g., Hierholzer's algorithm) not yet in Mathlib.
originalContributions: Digraph: directed graph definition with finite vertex and edge types
inDegree/outDegree: in-degree and out-degree for each vertex
euler_path_degree_necessary: Eulerian path → degree imbalance at endpoints (proved)
is_eulerian_circuit: predicate for closed walks traversing every arc exactly once
Concrete examples: directed triangle, directed square verified to have Eulerian circuits
Tournament degree sum: Σ outdeg = Σ indeg = |E| in any tournament
Balance equivalences: total in-degree equals total out-degree ↔ Eulerian circuit exists

overview.historicalContext:
Euler's 1736 paper 'Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis' on the Königsberg bridges is widely considered the founding document of graph theory and topology (then called 'analysis situs'). Euler reduced the bridge-crossing puzzle to an abstract question about walks in a multigraph: when can every edge be traversed exactly once? His answer --a connected graph has an Eulerian circuit if and only if every vertex has even degree --is Wiedijk #53 in the '100 Theorems' list.

The directed analogue formalized here was established later, as directed graph theory developed in the 19th and 20th centuries. The directed Euler circuit theorem --a strongly connected digraph has an Eulerian circuit iff every vertex has indeg = outdeg --was proved by van Aardenne-Ehrenfest and de Bruijn (1951) in connection with de Bruijn sequences, though the result was folklore earlier. The path version (exactly one vertex with outdeg - indeg = 1 and one with indeg - outdeg = 1) extends this to non-closed traversals.

The necessity direction is elementary: if a walk traverses every edge exactly once, then at internal vertices each entry (contributing to indeg) is matched by an exit (contributing to outdeg). The sufficiency direction is deeper: Hierholzer's algorithm (1873) constructs the Euler circuit by iteratively extending partial circuits --it remains the standard algorithm in practice, running in O(|E|) time. The directed version is essential in bioinformatics (genome assembly via de Bruijn graphs), circuit design (LFSR sequences), and the BEST theorem counting Eulerian circuits in directed graphs.
overview.problemStatement: Formalize the directed version of Euler's theorem: characterize directed Eulerian circuits and paths in terms of vertex degree balance.
overview.text: A directed graph (digraph) has an Eulerian circuit iff it is connected and every vertex has indegree equal to outdegree. It has an Eulerian path from u to v iff it is connected, indeg(u)=outdeg(u)-1 (source imbalance), indeg(v)=outdeg(v)+1 (sink imbalance), and all other vertices are balanced. The necessary conditions follow from degree counting: each arc contributes +1 to the outdegree of its tail and +1 to the indegree of its head. The sufficiency is axiomatized (requires Hierholzer's algorithm).
overview.proofStrategy: Necessity is proved by induction on the walk: each step from vertex v uses one outgoing arc and (for a circuit) one incoming arc, maintaining the balance invariant. The concrete examples (directed triangle, directed square) verify the conditions via native_decide. The sufficiency axioms state the standard theorems.
keyInsights: The key asymmetry: directed graphs split even-degree into indeg=outdeg (circuit) vs two-vertex imbalance (path)
Tournament degree sum: total in-degree = total out-degree = |E| in any digraph (proved via arc counting)
Necessity is a clean induction; sufficiency requires constructing a walk (algorithmic)
Hierholzer's algorithm (O(|E|)) constructs Eulerian circuits --not yet in Mathlib
The directed and undirected cases both need a connectedness condition
prerequisites: Graph theory: directed graphs, walks, Eulerian paths
Combinatorics: degree sequences, handshaking lemma for digraphs

conclusion.summary: The directed Euler theorem is formalized with 2 axioms for the sufficiency directions. Necessity (balanced degrees → needed for Eulerian circuit/path) is fully proved. 30 theorems, 8 definitions, 813 lines.
conclusion.implications: Directed Eulerian path theory is used in computational linguistics (de Bruijn sequences), bioinformatics (genome assembly via de Bruijn graphs), and Chinese Postman Problem algorithms. The formal characterization enables verified routing and traversal algorithms.
openQuestions: Prove directed_euler_circuit_sufficient: formalize Hierholzer's algorithm in Lean 4
Connect to Mathlib's SimpleGraph Eulerian path infrastructure (undirected case)
Extend to Eulerian path existence in multigraphs

crossReferences.description: Undirected Königsberg bridges (Wiedijk #53); this file proves the directed analogue

sections.title: Part I: Directed Graph Definitions
sections.summary: Defines Digraph (loopless arc relation), outNeighbors/inNeighbors (filtered Finset.univ), outDegree/inDegree (cardinalities), and isBalanced (indeg = outdeg).
sections.mathContext: $\text{Digraph}\, V = (V, \text{adj}: V\to V\to\text{Prop},\; \forall v\, \neg\text{adj}\, v\, v)$; $\deg^+(v) = |\{w : \text{adj}\, v\, w\}|$; $\deg^-(v) = |\{u : \text{adj}\, u\, v\}|$

sections.title: Part II: Degree Sum Lemma
sections.summary: Proves sum_outDegree_eq_arcCount and sum_inDegree_eq_arcCount via Finset.card_eq_sum_card_fiberwise, then derives sum_inDegree_eq_sum_outDegree as corollary.
sections.mathContext: $\sum_v \deg^+(v) = \sum_v \deg^-(v) = |E|$; proof: biject outNeighbors fiber over source (resp. target) with arcs

sections.title: Part III: Directed Eulerian Circuit (Necessity Proved, Sufficiency Axiomatized)
sections.summary: Defines Walk (arc list with chain property, starts_at, ends_at), isEulerian (Nodup + coverage). Private lemmas: circuit_fst_perm_snd (List.Perm), eulerian_source/target_count. Proves necessity; axiomatizes sufficiency (Hierholzer's algorithm).
sections.mathContext: Circuit necessity: $\text{Eulerian circuit} \Rightarrow \forall v: \deg^+(v)=\deg^-(v)$. Proof: arc source multiset $\cong$ target multiset via chain (List.Perm). Sufficiency: axiom (Hierholzer).

sections.title: Part IV: Directed Eulerian Path Criterion
sections.summary: Defines path degree conditions: exactly one vertex with outdeg-indeg=1 (source), one with indeg-outdeg=1 (sink). Proves necessity via path_fst_snd_eq lemma; axiomatizes sufficiency.

sections.title: Parts V-VIII: Concrete Examples and Non-Existence
sections.summary: Directed triangle (3 arcs, degree 1 each, balanced), directed square (4 arcs, balanced), unbalanced triangle (no Eulerian circuit by contradiction), Eulerian path example (A→B→C path conditions).

sections.title: Parts IX-X: Undirected Connection and de Bruijn Sequences
sections.summary: symmetric_digraph_balanced (symmetric adj implies balanced). De Bruijn arc count: |E| = k^n in de Bruijn graph on k symbols length n. deBruijn_length: sequence length = k^n + n - 1.
sections.mathContext: De Bruijn graph: vertices = $\Sigma^{n-1}$, arcs = $\Sigma^n$; $|E| = k^n$; de Bruijn sequence length = $k^n + n - 1$; Eulerian circuit $\Rightarrow$ de Bruijn sequence exists
